# Sam Altman faces fierce backlash after saying society must accept ‘Bad Things’ for AI progress

A demonstrators wearing a cut-out mask of CEO of OpenAI Sam Altman lights a smoke flare during a protest march against the construction of new data centers in Rho, near Milan, Italy, on October 3, 2026. Picture: PIERO CRUCIATTI / AFP

Image: PIERO CRUCIATTI / AFP

Recently, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman stirred controversy by asserting that society needs to accept that "bad things" must happen for artificial intelligence to advance. That stance reflects a callous, out-of-touch, and power-hungry mindset that elicits far more public concern than optimism for our technological future.

Altman argued that because humanity will inevitably use AI to generate orders of magnitude more good than harm, the collective benefits easily outweigh the fallout.

Yet that line of reasoning mirrors the perilous logic historically behind major global conflicts: the dangerous conviction that individual suffering and human sacrifice can simply be written off as collateral damage for an abstract "greater good.”

In truth, the loss of human safety and livelihood is never so easily dismissed. While tech executives may claim they are not literally dealing in life-or-death scenarios, the stakes with advanced machine intelligence are virtually limitless.

## Tech Leaders’ Push for Autonomy Sparks Debate Over AI Oversight and Safety

Figures like Sam Altman and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg consistently push back against external oversight and gatekeeping, driven by a desire for unrestricted autonomy within their executive suites. Operating behind closed doors gives corporate giants free rein to pursue aggressive, self-serving agendas while leaving everyday citizens completely in the dark regarding systemic risks.

Altman continues to advocate for a flexible, self-policing framework rather than binding government regulations aimed at mitigating risk, insisting that safety boundaries can easily prevent catastrophic, existential collapse. That proposed distinction is a perilous grey area. It immediately brings to mind classic dystopian warnings like in the movie Terminator , where an unchecked system slips beyond human control. While Hollywood fiction is dramatic, the core dilemma remains very real: cutting-edge AI can easily be leveraged to advance the agendas of those who wield the most leverage and capital. When corporate architects are granted unchecked freedom, the public has no way to guarantee their long-term motives remain ethical or safe.

Unsurprisingly, Altman’s comments have triggered severe backlash across the technology sector. Industry skeptics and governance advocates have condemned his remarks as tone-deaf, rightly arguing that private software developers should never be the arbiters of how much harm, scam activity, or collateral damage society is forced to absorb. That decision cannot belong to unilateral tech executives.

True innovation requires stringent accountability whenever deployments go wrong. Yet, with rapid advancements in AI models, tracing financial exploitation, deceptive scams, and cyber warfare back to responsible human actors is growing exceedingly difficult due to the complex, opaque nature of these tools.

By contrast, competitors such as Anthropic have embraced an appreciably different philosophy, emphasising deliberate development timelines, heightened caution, and tighter preventative safety protocols. That disciplined model represents a much more principled, responsible path forward for the industry.

Ultimately, tech leaders cannot be granted unlimited clearance to deploy volatile technologies simply because they have billions of dollars of capital to shield their operations. Rather than being handed total operational impunity, the architects of AI need to be held to rigorous, enforceable standards.
